title: Talent Retention in a World of Fast Movers
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article tackles talent retention against the backdrop of shortened average tenure (roughly four years per role). The author identifies two root drivers of restlessness — being over-challenged or under-challenged — and argues leaders should focus retention effort on high performers who crave more challenge rather than trying to save every departing employee. Three specific retention strategies are outlined: pairing high performers with other high performers, feeding them frequent developmental feedback, and continually raising the difficulty bar. The piece closes by framing great organizations as those that counter turnover trends by making the current role compelling enough that people don't need to leave for the next thing.
points: Team members typically start considering a change when they feel either overwhelmed (asked to do too much) or under-challenged (asked to do too little).

High-talent team members are retained through three specific strategies: connecting them with other high performers, feeding them frequent developmental feedback, and continually raising the bar of challenge.
Losing overwhelmed, low-skill/low-attitude team members isn't necessarily a bad outcome — retention effort should be targeted at high performers who want to be pushed.
Great organizations counter the 'job-hopping every four years' trend not by accepting it, but by proactively giving top talent a compelling reason to stay now.
quotes: Leaders and team members no longer stay in the same seats for very long. They change jobs or roles on average every four years or so.
Either they are being asked to do too much or too little. In other words, they are either challenged beyond their comfort zone, or they aren’t challenged enough to grow.
Because high talent is attracted to and benefits from other high talent, good leaders seek out opportunities to expose, connect, and couple the most talented team members.
High-talent team members also desire feedback. They look for information that can propel them forward and fast-track their development.
They fight the expectations team members have of always moving to the next thing by giving them a great thing now.
